analysis.one_liner: Permanently classifies broadband as lightly regulated, barring FCC common-carrier rules.
analysis.headline: The bill died in the House Energy and Commerce Committee without a hearing, markup, or vote, after drawing only two cosponsors.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill writes broadband Internet access into the Communications Act as a lightly regulated "information service" and states that broadband providers can never be treated as common carriers. That would permanently take away the Federal Communications Commission's strongest legal tool for governing Internet providers, including any open-internet (net neutrality) rules, and leave only weak authority to act. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and its communications subcommittee, and no further action was ever taken.
analysis.who_benefits: Broadband and cable Internet providers. The bill would lock their industry into the light-touch regulatory category by statute, ending any possibility that the FCC could reclassify broadband under common-carrier rules, impose net neutrality requirements, or regulate rates. The bill's own findings argue this protects the investment that built the networks [S3].

how_it_helps.text: The bill adds broadband to the legal definition of an "information service" and excludes providers of information services or advanced telecommunications capability from the definitions of "common carrier," "telecommunications carrier," and "telecommunications service" under the Communications Act [S2][S3].

It prohibits any provider of an information service from being treated as a telecommunications carrier or from being required to offer its service as a telecommunications service, blocking common-carrier treatment by statute rather than leaving it to FCC decisions [S2][S3].

The bill's findings argue that common-carrier (Title II) obligations would "severely harm broadband investment" and that prior FCC information-service rulings "unleashed tens of billions of dollars" in network investment [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Internet users. The bill would eliminate, by statute, the possibility of common-carrier protections for broadband — the legal foundation for enforceable open-internet rules and basic carrier duties — leaving the FCC with only narrow "ancillary jurisdiction" to regulate Internet access [S2]. Online content and service companies could face paid-prioritization deals or degraded service without a common-carrier backstop.
analysis.who_pays_short: Internet users and online content companies

drawbacks.text: The strongest good-faith objection to common-carrier regulation, stated in the bill's own findings, is that Title II-style rules could deter the network investment that builds and upgrades broadband [S3].

The cost an honest supporter must acknowledge: the bill would not merely set policy for now but would amend the Communications Act so broadband can never be a common-carrier service, permanently foreclosing the strongest consumer-protection tool the FCC has and leaving only narrow general authority to regulate Internet access [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill gives broadband providers regulatory certainty and, by its own argument, protects investment incentives. But its core effect is to write the industry's preferred legal category into statute, taking the open-internet question off the table for good: consumers would keep only the FCC's weak "ancillary jurisdiction," while the common-carrier framework that governs telephone service would be permanently out of reach [S2]. Weighing industry certainty against that permanent loss of protection, the costs fall on the public.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its communications subcommittee, and sat there until the Congress ended with no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

narrative.text: Rep. Robert Latta introduced the bill on May 28, 2014, and it was referred to the House Committee on Energy and Commerce the same day [S1][S5].

Two days later it was referred to the Subcommittee on Communications and Technology, where the record ends — no hearing, markup, committee vote, or floor action followed before the 113th Congress ended [S5].
The bill drew only two cosponsors, one Republican and one Democrat [S4].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Broadband providers did not get the statutory guarantee they sought, and because the bill died the FCC kept its authority to decide how broadband is classified and regulated, leaving open-internet policy unresolved rather than locked against common-carrier rules by law. Consumers and open-internet advocates were better off that the statute was never changed.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Broadband providers, avoided statutory lock-in? No — consumers kept FCC authority

for.name: Rep. Robert E. Latta
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill and sent it to the House Energy and Commerce Committee.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.what_they_did: Held the bill after referral and never reported it out; no hearing or markup is recorded.

against.name: Subcommittee on Communications and Technology
against.role: House Energy and Commerce subcommittee of referral
against.what_they_did: Received the bill on May 30, 2014, and took no further action on it for the rest of the Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only two House members cosponsored the bill — one Republican and one Democrat — and it never reached a vote, so the record shows no measurable partisan pattern either way [S4][S5].

industries.note: The bill would write the industry's preferred light-touch classification into statute, permanently removing the threat of common-carrier rules, net neutrality mandates, or rate oversight. Its interest in avoiding those obligations runs against the public's interest in an enforceable open internet.

industries.industry: Online content and edge providers (streaming, web services, startups)
industries.note: Without a common-carrier backstop, Internet access providers could charge for faster lanes or slow rivals' traffic, costs that fall on both edge companies and the people who use their services. These companies' interest in open access runs alongside the public's.
